[A1, F1, F2, construct]

Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto $q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology. [F2, construct]

Near any pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact, Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient addition law. The finite product is compact by [F3], connected by [F3], and abelian coordinatewise. It is therefore a compact connected abelian Lie group, hence a torus by [F4], of dimension $r$. The coordinate curves $\gamma_i(s)=(0,\ldots,[s],\ldots,0)$ are smooth group homomorphisms by the quotient charts and coordinate group law, so [F9] applies. Their derivatives at zero form the coordinate basis of $T_0T$, and $\gamma_i(s+1)=\gamma_i(s)$, so each has period one. For $T$, index product cells by subsets $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension $|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals; identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map $q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube, then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$ is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. Together with the cofibration from step 4.1, [F8] shows that the based group is well-pointed. [F3, F8, step 4.1, construct] ∎
